structured_output.summary: The search found 17 sourced claims, all from CIFAR-10 sources, general papers or the official benchmark repo. No public CIFAR-100 result faster than about 8 s exists to compare against. (1) Exact settings from the Hiverge and airbench94_muon scripts. Both freeze the BN weight and use eps 1e-12. Hiverge renormalizes weights every 4 steps, schedules a target update magnitude from 0.50 to 0.079, uses SGD momentum 0.825, label smoothing 0.09, SiLU, and linear decay to 0 with no warmup. airbench94_muon applies no weight decay to Muon weights, and its per-step renorm would cancel any decay anyway. (2) Cheaper Muon: Turbo-Muon reuses the AOL Gram matrix in the first NS step. Gram Newton-Schulz cuts FLOPs for wide matrices like ours, but is unstable at 2-3 iterations without a restart. Polar Express's first-step slope (8.29 vs 3.44) would lift small singular values more. Another paper finds that more exact orthogonalization does not reliably help training. (3) Margin sources: airbench's alternating-flip ablation (15% epoch-equivalent at 10 epochs without TTA) gives a strong prior for H1.2.1. Online label smoothing (+1.1 pp over plain smoothing on a CIFAR-100 ResNet-56) is a candidate that costs no time. CIFAR-100's 20 coarse labels could feed an auxiliary loss, if RULES.md allows it. (4) Transfer and noise: Fable's audit found CUDA-graph and foreach gains to be about 5 ms or net-neutral after fair re-timing, while progressive resizing was real. The A100 PCIe vs SXM power and bandwidth gap is confirmed. PyTorch docs confirm that cuDNN benchmark selection can pick different algorithms run to run. That fits H4.4(b) and E043.

findings.claim: Hiverge's CIFAR-10 recipe (94.02% in 1.98 s): Muon lr 0.205, momentum 0.655, Nesterov. Weights are renormalized every 4 steps, not every step ('normalization frequency 4'), toward a target magnitude that decays linearly from 0.5012 to 0.0786. 3 unrolled NS iterations with coefficients a=3.4576, b=-4.7391, c=2.0843. Weight decay 1.0418e-6 x batch. SGD for biases/head: momentum 0.825, bias lr 0.0573, head lr 0.5415. Linear warmdown to 0 with no warmup and no Lookahead. Label smoothing 0.09. BN momentum 0.5566 (Hiverge's convention; PyTorch momentum = 1 - 0.5566), eps 1e-12, weight frozen (bias only). SiLU activation. Widths 64/256/256. Whitening bias trained for 0.2 epoch. Brightness jitter 0.1399, contrast jitter 0.1308. ~7.65 epochs at batch 1536. TTA only on the 25% least-confident samples (banned here).
findings.relevance: Gives exact values for several knobs the tree inherited but never varied: the SGD-group momentum (0.825 vs ours), renorm frequency, the magnitude-target schedule, BN frozen weight and eps, and activation. It sizes the H1.3.5 jitter and the H2.5.3 renorm cadence. Hiverge has no Lookahead or warmup, so it is the reference point for H1.7.10.

findings.claim: airbench94_muon has BatchNorm momentum 0.6 (PyTorch 0.4), eps 1e-12, and weight.requires_grad=False. Before each Muon update, p.data is rescaled to norm sqrt(rows). Muon params get no weight decay; wd=2e-6*batch applies only to the SGD groups (bias_lr 0.053, head_lr 0.67). Label smoothing 0.2, batch 2000, 8 epochs, linear decay to 0, whitening bias trained for 3 epochs, logits divided by the final width, GELU, alternating flip, translate 2.
findings.relevance: With per-step renorm, decoupled weight decay on Muon weights only rescales them, and the renorm undoes it. Muon-weight wd is then a dead knob (my inference from the code). So in H1.7.12 only the SGD-group wd and the 64x BN-bias LR can matter. Also, if our port's BN weight is trainable or eps differs from 1e-12, that is an untested difference from both references.

findings.claim: Gram Newton-Schulz iterates on the small n x n Gram matrix R = XX^T instead of the n x m matrix X and applies the accumulated polynomial Q to X once at the end. The result is mathematically identical. Cost for T iterations is (4T + 6α - 6)n^3 vs T(3α+1)n^3 for symmetric NS, with α = m/n. Caveats: in bf16, spurious negative eigenvalues of R grow exponentially. The blog says naive Gram NS is unstable within 2-3 steps in its tests and recommends fp16, a safety factor of 1.05 and a restart after iteration 2. For T<=3 it suggests falling back to standard NS.
findings.relevance: Our conv matrices have α≈9 (576x5184, 384x3456, 128x1152). By my count, a 2-step Gram form would need ~22 n^3 vs ~38 n^3 for standard NS. Muon is ~1.5 ms/step (~0.5 s per trial), so the possible saving is ~0.1-0.2 s, but stability at T=2 in fp16 must be checked on captured real gradients. This would be a new H2.5 child that removes work and so should carry over to the judge.

findings.claim: In Turbo-Muon Algorithm 2, the Gram matrix A0 = X0^T X0 computed for AOL is reused for the first NS iteration as A1 = s^T A0 s, with no second Gram matmul. In the CIFAR-10 speedrun, Turbo-Muon gets 94.03% in 1.348 s vs Muon+ 94.04% in 1.359 s (-0.8%). It removes one of the usual 5 NS iterations.
findings.relevance: If our E024 implementation computes the Gram for the AOL scaling and then recomputes XX^T in the first NS step, reusing it saves one large matmul per parameter per step. That cut needs no accuracy check. Separately, Turbo-Muon's small speedrun gain (0.8%) suggests further NS cuts are worth only about 1%.

findings.claim: Polar Express recommends lower bound l=1e-3 (bf16) and upper u=1, T=5-6 for deep learning, and says an order-of-magnitude error in l only delays convergence by a few iterations. The first-iteration coefficients are (8.287, -23.596, 17.300), so the polynomial's slope at 0 is 8.29, vs 3.4445 for the standard Jordan quintic. It deflates every polynomial by a safety factor of 1.01 (x -> p(x/1.01)) and normalizes the input by ||M||_F + 1e-2.
findings.relevance: E035 failed because small singular values were not lifted. A minimax 2-step schedule starting with a slope near 8 lifts tiny singular values ~2.4x more per step than our coefficients. This supports trying H1.7.9 with recomputed 2-step coefficients, and possibly H6.2.1 (a 3rd step) without the extra matmul cost.

findings.source: arxiv.org/abs/2606.00371 (How Much Orthogonalization Does Muon Need?)
findings.claim: Training quality is not monotonic in polar-decomposition accuracy. A 5-step cubic NS (10 matmuls) matches the Muon-Jordan quintic (15 matmuls) within ~1e-3 validation loss from GPT-2 Small up to 4B models. Truncated Polar Express, Jordan quintic and cubic5 reach nearly identical final losses.
findings.relevance: This argues against H6.2, that orthogonalization quality caps accuracy once the basic lift is adequate. It suggests a 3rd NS step (H6.2.1) will likely add <0.1 pp. E035's 1-step failure is a different regime, because there the lift was inadequate.

findings.claim: Fable's CIFAR-10 record is 1.828 s at 94% vs Hiverge's 1.978 s (-7.6%, 200 trials each). The genuine gains came from progressive resizing: adding a 28->32 curriculum saved 0.128 s and deepening it to 24->28->32 saved another 0.081 s, with a per-epoch schedule of [24,24,24,28,28,28,32,32,32] (3 epochs at 32 px). The schedule was compressed to 9.0-9.75 epochs. CUDA-graph capture saved only ~5 ms, and graph plus foreach fusion was 'net neutral' (it looked ~0.04 s slower) once measured fairly. Gaming excluded from the legitimate score: moving augmentation/whitening out of the timed region (~150 ms), filtering for fast hosts (~20 ms), and a 60 s thermal cooldown (~9 ms). The global amax pool replacing MaxPool2d(3) made no difference at 32 px (2.298 vs 2.283 s).
findings.relevance: Supports H5: launch-overhead wins are tiny or unstable under fair timing, while pixel and work removal transfers. Fable spends only 3 of 9 epochs at 32 px, more aggressive than our 4 of 11. This bears on H2.3.2 (E037's 3x32 was inconclusive). Pooling was neutral at 32 px in Fable but -0.19 s in E042 here, because our cut replaced the atomic adaptive_max_pool2d backward.

findings.claim: Alternating-flip ablation on CIFAR-10 without TTA: equivalent to a 15.0% speedup at 10 epochs (airbench94), 27.1% at 20 epochs and 38.3% at 40 epochs. Adding Cutout or TTA shrinks the gain. On ImageNet it beats random flip in every setting where flipping helps. airbench96, without retuning, reaches 79.76% on CIFAR-100 vs 78.04% for ResNet-18 with Cutout.
findings.relevance: Gives a strong prior for H1.2.1. At ~10 epochs, random flip should cost about 15% of the epochs, i.e. ~1.3 epochs, which on our slope is likely >=0.3 pp. Alternating flip is then probably a real margin source, not a cost. The airbench96 transfer result also suggests bigger airbench nets carry over to CIFAR-100 without retuning (H6 capacity).

findings.claim: Official CIFAR-100 speedrun: one A100 80GB PCIe with MIG disabled, PyTorch 2.4.0, 40 official trials, mean prepare+train time, eval <=5 s per trial. The baseline ResNet9 scores 75.36% at 59.30 s. The repo has no PRs, open or closed, so no public faster record. abdullah-athar's PR #3 reports 75.29% (sd 0.25 pp) at 8.11 s (sd 0.02 s) over 40 trials on an A100-SXM4, and says Muon lost to SGD at every size in their tests. Search snippets also show an older rule version with an L40S and 50 trials.
findings.relevance: Confirms H5's judge (PCIe, 40 trials) and that no public CIFAR-100 recipe faster than ~8 s exists to borrow from. PR #3's per-seed sd of 0.25 pp matches our 0.28 pp (E046). Their 'Muon loses' finding contradicts E007; the likely reason is untuned Muon or a different batch.

findings.claim: Online label smoothing (OLS) keeps a K x K per-class soft-label matrix built from the predicted distributions of correctly classified training samples in the previous epoch (uniform in the first epoch). Loss = 0.5*CE(hard) + 0.5*CE(soft), with no extra forward passes. CIFAR-100 top-1 error: ResNet-56 26.81 hard, 26.37 uniform LS, 25.24 OLS; ResNeXt29-2x64d 20.92 / 20.34 / 18.81. That is a 1.1-1.5 pp gain over uniform LS, but measured on long (~200-epoch) schedules.
findings.relevance: A time-free margin source the tree has not considered, fitting H1.3/H6 ('margin from output settings'). It can be implemented inside the CUDA graph as a 100x100 buffer updated by scatter-add (reset in prepare). The gain at an 11-epoch schedule is unknown, likely much smaller. It would be a new H1.3 child.

findings.claim: CIFAR-100's 20 coarse superclass labels can be used through hierarchical label smoothing (smoothing mass spread only within the true superclass) or a second head with loss (1-λ)L_fine + λL_coarse. Both are reported to improve CIFAR-100 classification and reduce cross-superclass confusions. Exact fine-accuracy gains at short schedules were not found.
findings.relevance: A possible time-free margin source (a 20-way head costs nothing). Legality depends on whether RULES.md counts coarse labels as part of the allowed 50k training set; it must be checked before any run. The evidence is weak.

findings.source: arxiv.org/html/2605.24770v1 (Muon in Vision Transformers: Optimizer-Recipe Interactions)
findings.claim: Under a full recipe (Mixup, CutMix, LS, RandAugment, random erasing), Muon gains while AdamW degrades. Mixing adds cross terms δ_i x_j^T that enrich the gradient span and prevent late-training spectral concentration. Muon's gains over AdamW on a conv net (Xception) were modest. No CIFAR-100 experiments.
findings.relevance: A weak counterpoint to H1.3 ('input regularization hurts at short schedules'): under Muon, mild input mixing may help rather than hurt. This is relevant to H1.3.5 (jitter sign) and H1.3.2 (cutout). It is ViT- and long-schedule evidence only.

findings.claim: CacheMuon reuses earlier steps' polar factors to warm-start or approximate the current step's orthogonalization, exploiting how much momentum matrices correlate over time. Conservative settings closely match fresh Muon on language and vision training with fewer orthogonalization FLOPs; aggressive settings lose modest quality. The abstract does not quantify iteration savings.
findings.relevance: Another way to cut Muon's fixed ~1.5 ms/step without E035's failure mode (the lift comes from the cached factor). Our momentum is low (0.655), so consecutive momentum matrices may correlate less than in LLM training. Treat as speculative.

findings.source: arxiv.org/abs/2603.28921 (Critical Damping as a Momentum Schedule)
findings.claim: Momentum schedule μ(t) = 1 - 2·sqrt(α(t)). On ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 (200-epoch cosine, SGD, 5 seeds) it reaches 90% 2.34x faster (1.71-2.86x, p=4e-4) but ends 0.46 pp lower. A hybrid that switches to constant μ=0.9 recovers final accuracy (95.45 ± 0.05%).
findings.relevance: Low transfer to Muon at ~350 steps. It suggests momentum mainly trades early speed against final accuracy, consistent with E040's flat momentum result. Small support for leaving H1.7.7 closed.

findings.claim: With cudnn.benchmark on, cuDNN times candidate algorithms for each new shape. Because of benchmarking noise it may pick different algorithms on later runs, even on the same machine. Setting benchmark=False makes the selection deterministic, though the chosen algorithm may still be nondeterministic unless cudnn.deterministic / use_deterministic_algorithms is set. Autotuning and compiler tuning are listed as sources of run-to-run variation.
findings.relevance: Documents the mechanism behind H4.4(b) and the E043 smoke-vs-official mismatch: occasional different kernel picks re-roll trajectories, while E038 = E046 was bit-identical. It favours salts plus dev seeds as replicates and warns against using repeated official runs for selection.

findings.claim: A100 SXM4 80GB: 400 W TDP, 2,039 GB/s. A100 PCIe 80GB: 300 W TDP (one source lists 250 W for PCIe; that likely refers to the 40GB card), 1,935 GB/s. No public per-model throughput comparison for small conv training at these power limits was found.
findings.relevance: Confirms the power and bandwidth gap in H5/H5.1. The magnitude for this workload has no external measurement, so H5.1's ranking rule (prefer cuts that remove work) is still unvalidated.

findings.claim: Agent-driven research on the CIFAR-10 Airbench96 task cut wall-clock by 4.59% under an external evaluator with legality checks. The abstract does not list the techniques.
findings.relevance: Shows that automated tuning of a mature airbench recipe yields only single-digit percent gains, consistent with the diminishing per-cut gains here (~1-4% each). The paper body is the place to look for which levers worked.
